newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq sets $906 mln for food imports under oil deal.
newsitem.headline: Iraq sets $906 mln for food imports under oil deal.

text.p: Iraq has earmarked $906 million for food imports under the second phase of its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations, according to documents obtained by Reuters on Sunday.

They show that the Iraqi government has allocated $414 million -- of the $1.32 billion Baghdad will have to spend after the oil sales -- for humanitarian goods like medicines and spare parts for water sanitation systems and electricity.
The remaining $906 million would be spent on food, according to the documents which are part of Iraq's food distribution plan approved by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Monday.

The oil-for-food deal, which allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months, went into effect last December and was renewed for another six months on June 8. But Iraq had delayed exports for the second phase to modify plans for aid distribution.
Iraq said on Sunday that it had sent several oil contracts to the United Nations for approval and it would start oil exports as soon as the United Nations put its signature on the contracts.
Baghdad will start buying the food once proceeds from the limited oil sales deal are placed in the U.N. escrow fund.
In the first distribution plan Iraq had allocated $870 million for food and $450 million for other humanitarian imports.
For Iraq's three nothern provinces, currently outside Baghdad's control, the plan earmaks a total of $260 million for food and relief imports.

There will be no change in the amount of food rations distributed at give-away prices to Iraqis monthly -- nine kg (19.8 lb) of wheat flour, 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) of rice, two kg (4.4 lb) of sugar and one kg (2.2 lb) of cooking oil. Soap, detergents, tea and salt were also included in the ration system.
Iraq has frequently complained about delay in the arrival of food and medical supplies purchased during the first six months of the deal. Baghdad blamed the delay on the United States and Britain.
Eric Falt, the spokesman for the U.N. humanitarian coordinator for Iraq, told Reuters that goods bought under the first phase of the oil plan were still arriving.
Falt said only 1.5 million tonnes of food out of the 2.3 million Iraq planned to buy in the first six months of the deal had reached the country.
